rejected.title: Bias and propaganda
card: Bias
Bias is a one-sided view. It comes from who made a source and why they made it.
Propaganda
Propaganda is made on purpose to persuade people to think or act in a certain way. Governments often use it in wartime.
Signs of bias or propaganda include loaded words, strong emotion, one side shown as good and the other as evil, and facts left out.
Bias can be there without anyone trying to persuade, as in a private diary. Propaganda is aimed at an audience on purpose, to change minds.
rejected.remember: All propaganda is biased, but not all bias is propaganda. Propaganda sets out to persuade.

a.q: Which description best fits a piece of propaganda?
opts: A poster made to persuade people to support a cause
A diary entry written to record a private memory
A map made to show the roads of a town
A table of figures collected for a census
a.why: Propaganda is made on purpose to persuade. The poster is made to win support. The diary entry may be one-sided, but it was not made to persuade an audience.
a.clue: Look for the source made to change what people think or do.

b.q: In wartime, a soldier writes in his private diary that the enemy are cowards. His government prints posters showing the enemy as monsters to get men to enlist. Which is correct?
opts: The diary shows bias, and the poster is propaganda
The diary is propaganda, and the poster shows bias
Both are propaganda, because both are one-sided
Only the poster is biased, as the diary is private
b.why: Both sources are one-sided, so both are biased. Only the poster was made on purpose to persuade an audience, so only it is propaganda. Being one-sided is not enough to make the diary propaganda, as no one was meant to be persuaded by it.
b.clue: Which source was made to change what other people do?

draft.title: Bias and propaganda
card: Bias
Bias is a one-sided view. It comes from who made a source and why they made it.
Propaganda
Propaganda is made on purpose to persuade people to think or act in a certain way. Governments often use it in wartime.
Signs of bias or propaganda include loaded words, strong emotion, one side shown as good and the other as evil, and facts left out.
A biased source can still be used as evidence. It can show what its maker wanted people to believe.
draft.remember: Ask who made the source and why. A one-sided source still shows a point of view.

a.q: Which description best fits a piece of propaganda?
opts: A poster made to persuade people to support a cause
A diary entry written to record a private memory
A map made to show the roads of a town
A table of figures collected for a census
a.why: Propaganda is made on purpose to persuade. The poster is made to win support. The diary entry may be one-sided, but it was not made to persuade a public audience.
a.clue: Look for the source made to change what people think or do.

b.q: During a war, a government publishes a poster showing the enemy as cruel monsters and its own soldiers as brave heroes. What is the most sensible use of the poster for a historian?
opts: Evidence of what the government wanted people to believe
Proof that the enemy really was cruel in every way
Useless, because a biased source tells us nothing
Proof that most people agreed with the government
b.why: The poster is one-sided, but it shows the message the government wanted to spread. It cannot prove the enemy's behaviour. A biased source is still useful evidence of a point of view, so it is not useless.
b.clue: A one-sided source can still show what its maker wanted others to think.

wants.why: It gives students a real example of one-sided persuasion to picture.
